entities.name: International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA), founded in 1927, serves as a pivotal organization in the global library and information sector. Headquartered in The Hague, Netherlands, IFLA emerged during a period of heightened international cooperation and modernization, reflecting the growing importance of information access and literacy in a rapidly changing world. Key figures such as the first president, Paul Otlet, and various national library associations have played critical roles in fostering collaboration among libraries worldwide, making IFLA a vital player in the promotion of library and information services across diverse cultures and regions.

From its inception, IFLA has championed initiatives that promote the value of libraries, including the establishment of standards and guidelines for library practices and the advocacy for universal access to information. The organization has held numerous World Library and Information Congresses, creating platforms for discourse on library science, information literacy, and digital access, which have evolved alongside technological advancements. IFLA’s commitment to preserving cultural heritage and supporting libraries in developing nations emphasizes its role in fostering equitable access to knowledge.

The legacy of IFLA is seen in the global standards for library services that continue to influence national policies and practices across the globe. Its efforts have not only transformed the landscape for library services but have also paved the way for new frameworks in information science and education. As libraries adapt to the digital age, IFLA’s commitment to professional development and international collaboration ensures that libraries remain relevant and impactful in society.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: IFLA significantly shaped global library practices and standards, influencing millions of library users and professionals worldwide. Its advocacy for universal access to information has led to more equitable knowledge dissemination across cultures.
